The views expressed in the publication are solely those of the named authors. This systematic review evaluates the health benefits of insulation against cold in residential environments. It was conducted to support the development of WHO’s Housing and Health Guidelines. The review aims to provide the best available evidence to inform the deliberations of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The report includes sections on the health effects of cold, eligibility criteria, search strategies, data extraction, findings, and comprehensive appendices. Previous research has shown that exposure to cold negatively impacts health. This review contributes to discussions on the role of housing in preventing such exposure. Two prior reviews addressed related topics, but this review focuses specifically on whether housing with better thermal insulation is healthier. The review also considers the broader issue of indoor temperature and health, which is addressed in a separate review. The research question for this review is: Do people living in insulated housing have better health outcomes than those in non-insulated housing? Eligibility criteria were based on a reduced set of inclusion criteria from previous studies. Studies that did not separate the effects of thermal envelope measures from heating measures were excluded. Health-related outcomes assessed include respiratory morbidity and mortality, all-cause infant mortality, hospital admissions, cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, depression, and high blood pressure. The review process involved searching for studies in major bibliographic databases, including PubMed, Web of Knowledge, and Google Scholar. The search aimed to avoid missing pivotal studies that could alter the findings or conclusions. The review incorporated studies identified in previous reviews and additional searches conducted in 2015 and 2018. The eligibility criteria were revised in 2018 to include studies where insulation was part of a broader home improvement package, even if the direct health effects of insulation could not be isolated. The review extracted information on study location, date, participants, intervention details, study design, and outcomes. Quality assessments were conducted, focusing on risk of bias, study quality, and relevance to the research question. Evidence profiles were completed for each study, summarizing the findings and their implications.
